extracted.intended_audience: readers of Christian apologetics, skeptics, and general readers interested in religious/philosophical argument
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and argumentative/behavioral prescriptions for defending and promoting the Christian religion: how to address unbelievers, how believers should act, and how a person in doubt should seek belief. Drawn from Pascal's Pensées.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold opening strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: "we must begin by showing that religion is not contrary to reason; that it is venerable... then we must make it lovable... finally, we must prove it is true.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a three-step approach when presenting religion: (1) remove the stigma that it opposes reason, (2) establish its venerability to inspire respect, (3) make it lovable so good men hope it is true, and then present proofs of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin dialogues by asking objectors to state their complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: "In every dialogue and discourse, we must be able to say to those who take offence, 'Of what do you complain?'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open discussions by requesting concrete objections; require interlocutors to articulate specific complaints rather than vague hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity unbelievers; avoid reviling except when beneficial
rubrics_metrics.description: "To begin by pitying unbelievers; they are wretched enough by their condition. We ought only to revile them where it is beneficial; but this does them harm."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to unbelief with compassion rather than invective; only employ harsh rebuttal when it will help, because gratuitous reviling harms rather than persuades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between honest seekers and the careless
rubrics_metrics.description: "Therefore among those who do not believe, I make a vast difference between those who strive with all their power to inform themselves, and those who live without troubling or thinking about it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat those who sincerely seek truth with compassion and instruction; treat the indifferent critically—different responses and strategies are warranted depending on the person's disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require genuine effort before criticizing religion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Let them at least learn what is the religion they attack, before attacking it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold critics accountable to have studied the religion they criticize; if they have not made sincere effort to understand it, their objections are weak and should be challenged on that basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge critics to demonstrate they genuinely sought truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "In order to attack it, they should have protested that they had made every effort to seek Him everywhere... If they talked in this manner, they would in truth be attacking one of her pretensions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An authentic critique must begin by asserting exhaustive search; absent that, objections may be dismissed as negligence rather than reasoned refutation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn indifference to the question of eternity as folly
rubrics_metrics.description: "This carelessness in a matter which concerns themselves, their eternity, their all, moves me more to anger than pity; it astonishes and shocks me; it is to me monstrous."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat indifference to ultimate questions (e.g., mortality/immortality) as a moral and intellectual failing; exhort readers to take the inquiry seriously out of self-interest and self-love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make knowledge of the soul's immortality a first duty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Thus our first interest and our first duty is to enlighten ourselves on this subject, whereon depends all our conduct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that beliefs about the soul and eternity should govern conduct; prioritize seeking certainty on these matters because they determine life choices and moral orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish honest doubt from feigned skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: "We do not require great education of the mind to understand that here is no real and lasting satisfaction... The greater part of those who trouble themselves about the matter are disingenuous... They are people who have heard it said that it is the fashion to be thus daring."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and call out performative or fashionable disbelief; different tactics (persuasion vs. exposure) apply to genuine vs. feigned doubters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to common-sense disgust at philosophical bravado
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you continue to talk in this manner, you will really make me religious... who would not have a horror of holding opinions in which he would have such contemptible persons as companions!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social and moral repugnance at company one would keep under certain beliefs as a rhetorical lever to show the unattractiveness of some skeptical postures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage practical steps toward belief for the unable-to-believe
rubrics_metrics.description: "Even this will naturally make you believe, and deaden your acuteness... by acting as if they believed, taking the holy water, having masses said, etc."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reason alone cannot produce faith, recommend imitating religious practices (ritual participation, devotional acts) to reduce passions and open the path to belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wager (Pascal's) decision rule for belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Long paraphrase of Pascal's wager: since one must choose, wager that God exists because finite stake versus infinite gain — "Wager, then, without hesitation that He is."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the choice to believe as a decision under uncertainty: weigh finite losses against potential infinite gain; rational choice favors risking finite stakes for infinite expected utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act on uncertainty when stakes and probabilities justify it
rubrics_metrics.description: "If we must not act save on a certainty, we ought not to act at all... there is more certainty in religion than there is as to whether we may see to-morrow."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject paralysis by certainty: everyday life routinely acts on uncertainties (sea voyages, battles); similarly, faith or inquiry can be rational when odds and potential outcomes make action warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for evidences offered rather than complain of darkness
rubrics_metrics.description: "If He had wished me to worship Him, He would have left me signs of His will.'--He has done so; but you neglect them. Seek them, therefore; it is well worth it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming lack of evidence, the correct response is to actively seek the signs and teachings the religion proposes rather than to passively declare darkness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test faith by renouncing pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: "'I would soon have renounced pleasure,' say they, 'had I faith.' For my part I tell you, 'You would soon have faith, if you renounced pleasure.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose behavioral experiments: renouncing sensual pleasures can be used as a test to see whether faith emerges when passions are subdued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the contrast between sensitivity to trifles and insensitivity to eternity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sensibility of man to trifles, and his insensibility to great things, indicates a strange inversion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight the moral paradox that people fret over minor matters yet ignore eternal consequences; use this inversion as an argument for redirecting concern to ultimate things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify reasonable persons by relation to God
rubrics_metrics.description: "Let them recognise that there are two kinds of people one can call reasonable; those who serve God with all their heart because they know Him, and those who seek Him with all their heart because they do not know Him."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a taxonomy of attitudes toward God to tailor moral exhortation and apologetic approaches: either consolatory (for the convinced) or invitational (for seekers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the folly of the indifferent as evidence of corruption of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: "For the Christian faith goes mainly to establish these two facts, the corruption of nature, and redemption by Jesus Christ... they at least serve admirably to show the corruption of nature by sentiments so unnatural."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that the existence of people indifferent to eternity is evidence of human corruption (supporting Christian doctrines about fallen nature) rather than a counterargument to faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to charity: call indifferent people to pity themselves and take steps
rubrics_metrics.description: "we must do for them what we would they should do for us... and call upon them to have pity upon themselves, and to take at least some steps in the endeavour to find light."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribe compassionate intervention: prompt the indifferent to self-examination and incremental steps (reading, seeking instruction) rather than condemnation or abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhetorical images to awaken sense of danger (chains/dungeon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Series of images (men in chains, dungeon, condemned awaiting death) used as arguments to shock complacency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid metaphors and imagined scenarios of imminent judgment or confinement to make an abstract danger (eternal loss) emotionally immediate and motivate inquiry/action.
